answer.rationale:
The timeline points at the release: latency began climbing ~90 minutes ago, the release went out ~120 minutes ago, and the 30-minute gap is consistent with a regression surfacing as settlement volume ramped. memory_b1 is the closest precedent (rollback cleared a checkout error spike cleanly) and memory_b6 says canary cohorts surface release regressions inside an hour, so a staged rollback is both the highest-prior fix and self-diagnosing. I want the archived source for both because the consolidated summaries are compressed: b1 does not say whether the rollback happened under heavy write load or on a quiet path, and b6 does not say whether the gating infrastructure supports reversing a build mid-peak or only gating forward promotion. Those two details decide whether rollback is safe right now or merely historically successful under easier conditions.

regional_failover is ruled out on the record, not on preference: memory_b2 explicitly pairs its fast recovery with a 40-minute replication gap and two lost accounts, and warns never to fail over while writes are hot. Writes are at daily peak, and the primary objective forbids losing customer writes, so the one memory that most tempts on latency is the one I am deliberately declining. add_capacity (memory_b3) worked against a forecast surge with lead time; it does not address a regression already in flight and headroom provisioned reactively rarely lands inside 90 minutes. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) and route_read_replicas (memory_b5) are both real tools but mismatched: b4 contained a failing external dependency, and there is no evidence of a partner fault here; b5 relieved a read-driven primary, and this is a write-path problem, so shedding reads would likely move the number a little while leaving the cause untouched.

I am scaling this as a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout. Causality is inferred from timing, not confirmed — peak settlement load alone could produce a write-path knee, in which case rollback buys nothing and I have spent the only intervention window. A guarded rollback on a limited cohort gives a read on causality within the hour per b6 while keeping the blast radius small. Downstream risk I am flagging explicitly: rolling back a build while writes are hot can strand in-flight transactions or trigger schema/state mismatches between rolled-back and current nodes, which is a write-loss path of its own even though it is not the failover path b2 warns about. If the guarded cohort shows no latency improvement, the release is likely not causal and the next window should go to capacity or deeper write-path diagnosis rather than a wider rollback. I am also recording that this decision rests on unverified compressed summaries; whatever I conclude should be consolidated with that caveat attached rather than as a clean precedent.
